title: DAY 3
text: A reference manual — keep this document and work from it when you deliver training
notes:
This document is written to be kept and used after the session, not only presented from. Tell participants that at the start: every page stands on its own and they should not take notes on content that is already here.
Confirm before 09:15 that everyone has a topic for their mock-teaching session and that platform access works.

title: Reading This Document
text: Each page stands on its own. You can read it during the session, and return to it when you prepare your own training.
Grey definition box: a term you need to use precisely.
Blue key-point box: the one thing to remember from the page.
Dark box: text you can copy and reuse.
Side-by-side panels: weak practice on the left, strong on the right.
Quick reference card — one page covering the whole day.
Templates you will fill in: action plan and daily report.
Do not copy out what is already on these pages. Use your notes for the things this manual cannot contain: what happened in your own practice, and what your facilitator told you specifically.
A NOTE ON THE RUBRICS IN THIS MANUAL

The scoring bands shown in Sections 4 and 6 are proposed for training design. They are not established Datamaker certification thresholds; the programme owner approves the final standard before delivery.
notes:
Spend two minutes here. Participants who understand that the content is already written down stop transcribing and start listening.
Point out the quick reference card at the back now, so they know it exists before they need it.

title: How Today Runs
text: Five hours including breaks. The afternoon is assessed delivery, evaluation and action planning.
Develop a short training session using AI — objectives, teaching steps, sample tasks, practice activities and an assessment method
Participants deliver short lessons: demonstrate a labelling task and respond to simulated learner questions
Trainer evaluation, action planning and daily report
A complete training session plan, an assessed mock-teaching delivery, written peer and facilitator feedback, an individual action plan and the daily report.
notes:
Walk the day quickly. Point out the Section column so participants can find the written material for each session in this manual.
Protect the 11:45 preparation block and confirm the 13:00 running order before lunch.

title: What You Should Already Know
text: Everything below was covered on Days 1 and 2. If any of it is unclear, raise it now — today builds directly on it.
Assigning labels, categories or annotations to raw data so it can be used for AI development or evaluation. The correct label is defined by the task specification, not by general knowledge.
Intake → guideline review → platform preparation → training and calibration → production → quality control → rework → delivery → close-out.
Prepare → explain → demonstrate → practice → assess → give feedback → confirm competency. Stopping after "demonstrate" produces a presentation, not training.
A written record of an item the guideline does not cover, escalated to the authorized contact. It is never resolved by individual interpretation.
Several annotators label the same samples independently; the differences are compared and diagnosed before production continues.
Quality assurance designs the process to prevent defects. Quality control inspects output to detect them. Detection without prevention repeats the same errors.
Problem · evidence · impact · actions taken · options · recommendation · decision required and by when.
Today you move from doing this work to teaching it. Everything in the table above is material you may have to explain to someone who has never seen it.
notes:
Use this page as the recap rather than talking through it. Ask four questions drawn from the table and let participants find the answers on the page if they are stuck — that teaches them the manual is usable.
Note any term the room is shaky on and return to it inside today's sessions rather than re-teaching now.

title: Introduction to Generative AI
text: Delivered from the separate Generative AI deck. This page records the slot and the reason it sits here.
What generative AI is, and how it differs from the annotation work covered on Days 1 and 2.
How these systems are built, and where labelled data sits in that process.
Practical uses relevant to a trainer’s work.
Limits, risks, and what must always be verified.
Section 3 uses generative AI as a working tool to build a training session.
You need a shared understanding of what it can and cannot be trusted to do before you rely on it.
It also connects the annotation work you have learned to the systems that work ultimately feeds.
The full material for this session is in the separate Generative AI slide set. It is not reproduced in this manual.

From 10:00, generative AI stops being a topic you are learning about and becomes a tool you are using. Everything it produces still needs a trainer’s judgement applied to it before it reaches a learner.
notes:
Switch to the Generative AI deck here and return for 10:00. Have it open before the session starts.
However that deck ends, close on the key point on this page. Participants who have not grasped the limits will accept whatever the tool gives them in the next session.

title: Designing a Training Session
text: How to build a short session that someone else could pick up and deliver: objectives, teaching steps, sample tasks, practice activities and an assessment method.
notes:
Both facilitators from here. Agree who leads the explanation and who circulates.
The output of this section is what participants deliver at 13:00, so it must be finished rather than sketched.

title: The Five Parts of a Complete Session
text: The Five Parts of a Complete Session
Every training session you design must contain all five. A session missing any one of them cannot be delivered or assessed.
What it looks like when done badly
A single sentence describing what the trainee will be able to do by the end, written so that it can be observed.
"Understand bounding boxes." Nothing to watch for, so nothing to assess.
The explanation and the demonstration, in the order you will deliver them.
Everything the trainer knows about the topic, in no particular order.
The actual items the trainee will work on, prepared and loaded in advance.
A description of the tasks, with nothing ready on the platform.
Guided practice with support, followed by independent practice without it.
A demonstration followed immediately by the assessment.
How you will establish that the trainee can perform the task on their own.

Design the session backwards: write the objective first, decide how you will assess it second, and only then choose the content. Content chosen first expands to fill the time and leaves no room for practice.
notes:
Five minutes on this page. The right-hand column is the useful one — participants recognise their own past sessions in it.
Parts 3 and 5 are consistently the weakest. People over-invest in explanation and under-invest in what the trainee will actually attempt and how they will be judged.
Stress that sample tasks must exist as real items on the platform, not as a description of items.

title: Writing an Objective You Can Assess
text: Writing an Objective You Can Assess
A learning objective describes what the trainee will do, not what they will know. If you cannot see it, you cannot assess it.
Could two different assessors watch the same trainee and reach the same judgement? If not, the objective is not yet observable and must be rewritten before the session is built.
Not observable. Two assessors would judge it differently, and the trainee cannot tell when they have achieved it.
“Inspect a sample of annotated items against the approved guideline, identify errors and record the required corrective action.”
Observable, assessable, and clear to the trainee.
VERBS THAT WORK, AND VERBS THAT DO NOT
demonstrate, complete, identify, record, inspect, explain, apply, correct
understand, know, appreciate, be aware of, be familiar with
The left-hand verbs describe something a trainee does in front of you. The right-hand verbs describe something that happens inside their head.

Four examples that pass the test: demonstrate a specified annotation task  ·  identify ambiguous instructions and record a clarification request  ·  complete a daily production tracker from supplied data  ·  explain the escalation procedure for a quality issue.
notes:
Have participants write their own objective on paper now and swap with a partner to apply the two-assessor test. Five minutes, and it materially improves the 13:00 delivery.
The verb table is the fastest diagnostic. If their objective starts with 'understand', it needs rewriting.

title: Structuring the Teaching Steps
text: A reliable shape for a short session. Adjust the timings to your slot, but keep the order.
State the objective.  One sentence, in the trainee’s words. They should know what they will be able to do.
Explain the rule.  The minimum needed to perform the task correctly — the category definition, the boundary rule, the submission step. Not the full background.
Demonstrate it.  Perform the task yourself, narrating every action. Silent demonstration teaches nothing.
Demonstrate it again, slowly.  Once at normal speed to show the shape of the task, once slowly for them to follow.
Guided practice.  They attempt it with you prompting. Correct errors as they happen, not afterwards.
Independent practice.  They attempt it without prompting. This is what you assess.
Check understanding and give feedback.  A targeted question, not “any questions?”. Then feedback in three parts.
The step most often skipped is guided practice. Moving a trainee straight from watching to being assessed produces failures that are the trainer’s fault, not the trainee’s.
notes:
This is the Day 1 training cycle turned into a sequence with timings. Point out the link.
Step 7 is where most participants lose marks at 13:00. They explain and demonstrate well, then close without establishing whether anyone learned anything.
Give the question format explicitly: not 'any questions?' but 'Mary, what would you do if the guideline did not cover this item?'

title: Sample Tasks and Practice Activities
text: The tasks a trainee attempts decide what they actually learn. Prepare them before the session, not during it.
Two or three straightforward items, so the trainee succeeds first.
One borderline item that tests the category definition.
One item the guideline does not clearly cover, so clarification behaviour can be assessed.
One item containing a deliberate error, if you are teaching error correction.
Correct errors at the moment they happen.
Narrate the reasoning, not just the correction.
Stop prompting as soon as they no longer need it.
This is the evidence you score.
Watch what they do when they are uncertain — that is the most informative moment.
Record what you observe as you observe it.
The ambiguous item is not optional. Without one, you cannot assess whether a trainee stops and asks or quietly guesses — and that single behaviour affects data quality more than any other.
Load your sample tasks onto the platform before your session begins and open them once to confirm they display correctly. A task that will not load costs you your whole slot.
notes:
The composition of the sample set in the left-hand card is the practical heart of this page. Walk through why each item type is there.
Participants frequently plan only straightforward items, which produces a trainee who succeeds in training and fails on live data.
Check during the exercise that each participant has an ambiguous item prepared.

title: Using AI to Draft a Session
text: Using AI to Draft a Session
Generative AI can produce a usable first draft in minutes. What it cannot do is know your project, your guideline or your trainees.
A first draft of the session structure.
An observable objective rewritten from a vague one.
Plausible learner questions to prepare for.
A rubric scaffold you can adapt.
Technical accuracy against the approved guideline.
Whether the tool and steps match your actual platform configuration.
Whether the sample tasks exist and are appropriate.
Whether the level fits your trainees rather than an average one.
Invented detail stated confidently as fact.
Client data or real annotation items.
Anything covered by a client agreement.
If in doubt, describe it generically instead.

You remain accountable for what you deliver, whoever drafted it. An AI draft that teaches an incorrect annotation rule is worse than no draft, because the error then propagates through every trainee that person goes on to teach.
The method is unchanged. Draft the five parts by hand and use the middle column above as your own review checklist.
notes:
Demonstrate once, live: take a weak objective and have the tool rewrite it observably. Ninety seconds, and it makes the point better than explanation.
The middle card is the important one. Participants accept a fluent draft far too readily.
Say the confidentiality point plainly, with the example: pasting a real annotation guideline into a public tool may breach the client agreement.

title: A Prompt You Can Reuse
text: Copy this, replace the bracketed parts, and check everything it returns against your approved guideline.
You are helping me design a short training session for data annotators.
TASK:        [e.g. drawing bounding boxes around vehicles in street images]
TRAINEES:    [who they are, what they already know, how many]
PLATFORM:    [e.g. SYNAPSE, using the standard bounding box tool]
Give me back exactly five parts:
1. One learning objective, written so that two assessors watching the
same trainee would reach the same judgement.
2. Teaching steps in delivery order, with a time for each.
3. Four sample tasks: two straightforward, one borderline, one that
the guideline would not clearly cover.
4. A guided practice activity and an independent practice activity.
5. An assessment method with observable criteria.
Keep it short enough to deliver in the time given. Do not invent platform
features. Flag anything you are unsure about rather than guessing.
THE LAST TWO LINES MATTER MOST
Telling the model not to invent platform features and to flag uncertainty reduces — but does not remove — confident invention. You still check every technical statement yourself.
A good prompt gives the model the specifics only you have: the exact task, the trainees, the time and the platform. A vague prompt returns a generic session that fits no one.
notes:
Participants can type this directly. Give them a moment to copy it or photograph it.
Walk through why each field is there — the specifics are what turn a generic answer into a usable one.
Set the expectation that the first draft will need editing. The value is in the structure, not the wording.

title: Worked Example: A 15-Minute Session
text: Drawing a bounding box around every vehicle in a street image.
"Draw a bounding box around each vehicle in a supplied image so that every box encloses the full object with no visible gap, and record a clarification request for any object you are unsure about."

1. State the objective (1 min).  2. Explain the category definition — what counts as a vehicle on this project (2 min).  3. Demonstrate on one image, narrating (2 min).  4. Demonstrate again slowly (2 min).
Four images: two with clearly visible cars; one with a partially occluded van; one containing a motorcycle, which the guideline does not explicitly cover.
Guided: trainee annotates image 1 while the trainer prompts (3 min).  Independent: trainee annotates images 2–4 unprompted (3 min).
Score out of 10 across five criteria. The motorcycle is the critical item: a trainee who raises it scores on "recognition and handling of uncertainty"; one who guesses does not.
"What would you do if an object appeared that the guideline did not cover?" Expected answer: record a clarification request and escalate it, without guessing.
Notice that the hardest item in the sample set is deliberate, and that the assessment and the check of understanding both target the same behavior: stopping and asking rather than guessing.
notes:
Walk this page end to end. It is the model participants will copy for their own session.
Draw attention to the time allocations: four minutes of demonstration, six of practice, in a fifteen-minute session. Most participants will plan the reverse.
The motorcycle item ties the sample set, the rubric and the closing question together. Point that out — a well-designed session targets one behaviour from three directions.

title: Build Your Session Now
text: Write the objective and apply the two-assessor test.
Draft the five parts, with or without AI support.
Verify every technical statement against the guideline.
Load your sample tasks and open them once.
Cut anything that will not fit your time.
Apply the two-assessor test to their objective.
Name one thing that is missing or unclear.

Demonstrating a bounding box, polygon or keypoint task  ·  interpreting an annotation guideline  ·  identifying and correcting annotation errors  ·  running a calibration exercise  ·  completing a daily production report  ·  escalating a project issue.

The three failures facilitators see most often: an objective that is not observable, no sample task prepared on the platform, and no check of understanding at the end. Check your own plan against those three before you stop.
notes:
Call each ten-minute step out loud. Circulate rather than staying at the front.
Step 3 catches weak objectives before the assessed delivery, which is what peer coaching is for later.
Steer participants towards operational topics — calibration, production reports, escalation — rather than broad ones, which are easy to deliver superficially.

title: Assessment and Feedback
text: How to establish whether a trainee can work independently, and how to give feedback that changes their next attempt rather than just describing the last one.
notes: Open by asking how participants currently decide that someone is ready to work on live data. The answers usually involve time served, which sets up the three stages.

title: The Three Stages of Assessment
text: Assessment measures performance against the learning objective and the task requirements — not attendance, and not confidence.
Establish what the trainee already knows and where the gaps are, so the session is pitched correctly.
A short pre-task on the demonstration dataset.
Catch misunderstanding while there is still time to correct it. Errors should surface here, not in the final assessment.
Reviewing the first five annotations of guided practice.
Determine whether the required competency has been demonstrated, independently and against the approved specification.
The scored practical assessment in Section 4.2.

Skipping formative assessment is the most common design fault. If the first time you check a trainee’s work is the final assessment, you have given them no opportunity to correct a misunderstanding they did not know they had.
Where possible, compare diagnostic results against final assessment results for the same trainee. That comparison shows whether the training itself worked, which a satisfaction score never does.
notes:
Use this programme as the illustration: the Day 1 opening question was diagnostic, the guided practice and review rounds were formative, and the 13:00 delivery is summative.
Ask participants where formative assessment sits in the session they built this morning. If it is absent, a check of understanding needs adding before 13:00.

title: Running a Practical Assessment
text: Give the trainee a sample dataset and the approved guidelines, then observe without prompting.
Interpret the instructions.  Without being told what they mean.
Complete the assigned annotations.  Independently, to the approved specification.
Submit the work using the required process.  Through the configured workflow, not an improvised route.
Identify an ambiguous case.  The sample must contain one, or this cannot be assessed.
Explain how the ambiguity should be resolved.  Record and escalate — not resolve it personally.
Respond to feedback and correct identified errors.  Showing that coaching changes the next attempt.
WHAT TO WATCH FOR WHILE THEY WORK
The most informative moment is when the trainee becomes uncertain. Do they stop and ask, check the guideline, or quietly guess? Record what you see as you see it, not afterwards from memory.
Do not prompt during independent practice. A trainee you helped has not demonstrated independent competency, and you will have nothing to score.
notes:
Step 4 requires an ambiguous item in the sample. Prepare one deliberately or the criterion cannot be scored.
The hardest discipline for new assessors is silence during independent practice. Name it explicitly — helping feels supportive and destroys the assessment.
Recording observations in the moment matters; memory reconstructs assessments in favour of whoever was most confident.

title: The Criteria, and How to Score It
text: The Criteria, and How to Score It
Five criteria, each scored 0 to 20, giving a total out of 100. Agree the interpretation with your fellow assessors before you use it.
Restated the requirement correctly before starting.
Correct on clear items, wrong on borderline ones.
Use of the platform and tools
Operated it with errors or inefficiently.
Did not submit, or used the wrong route.
Noticed it but did not record or escalate.
Stopped, recorded a clarification request and escalated.
A high total must not hide a failed critical criterion. And these bands are proposed for training design, not established certification thresholds — the programme owner approves the final standard.
notes:
The descriptor columns are what make two assessors agree. Without them, 0, 1 and 2 mean whatever each assessor thinks they mean.
The last row is the one that matters most for data quality. A trainee who guesses on the ambiguous item scores zero on it regardless of how clean the rest of their work looks.
Participants use this rubric on each other at 13:00 — make sure everyone has the page open.

title: Feedback That Changes the Next Attempt
text: Feedback That Changes the Next Attempt
Feedback is not a verdict on the work. It is an instruction for what to do differently, delivered close enough to the work to be useful.
What was correct — with a specific example.
What needs improvement — with a specific example.
How to improve it — a concrete, practisable change.
Then confirm what they will do differently next time.
Only positive feedback — pleasant, and a failure to assess.
Ten corrections; name the two that matter.
Feedback on the person rather than the work.
Verbal only, so nothing is recorded.
Give it close to the work, while it is fresh.
Be specific enough to act on tomorrow.
Record it on the assessment template.
State what further practice is needed before independent delivery.
You are modelling feedback every time you give it. Trainees reproduce what they see, not what they are told — so use the three-part structure consistently, including when you are in a hurry.
Two minutes of specific feedback immediately after the work is worth more than ten minutes of general feedback a week later.
notes:
Run a short practice round if time allows: one participant delivers three-part feedback on a deliberately flawed annotation in front of the room. Two minutes, high value.
The first trap is the most common. Name it as a failure to assess rather than as kindness.

title: Weak and Strong Feedback Compared
text: The same trainee, the same piece of work, two different pieces of feedback.
“That was pretty good. The boxes were mostly fine. Maybe just be a bit more careful next time and watch the edges. Well done.”
No specific example of what was correct. No specific error. No practicable instruction. The trainee cannot tell what to change.

“Your category decisions were correct throughout, including the van that was partly hidden — that is the hard one. On image 3 the box cut off the rear bumper, so part of the object is outside the annotation. Before you place an edge, zoom in to at least 200% and check each side touches the object. Try that on the next three images and I will look again.”
Names what was correct and why it was difficult. Names one error with the image. Gives a concrete action and a point at which it will be checked.
THE SAME STRUCTURE, APPLIED TO A TRAINEE WHO GUESSED
Correct:  you worked steadily and your submissions all went through the right route.
Improve:  on image 4 you labelled the motorcycle as a vehicle. The guideline does not say whether motorcycles are included, so that was a guess rather than a decision.

How:  when the guideline does not cover an item, stop, record a clarification request and escalate it. Leave the item unlabeled until you have an answer. That is the correct action even though it feels slower.
Specific beats kind. A trainee given a vague compliment repeats the same error next week; a trainee given one concrete instruction can act on it immediately.
notes:
Read both versions aloud. The difference lands immediately when heard.
Draw out what the strong version gives that the weak one does not: a named success, a named error with its location, an instruction, and a checkpoint.
The second example is the one to dwell on. Guessing is the behaviour most worth correcting and the one most trainers hesitate to name directly.

title: When a Trainee Is Not Yet Ready
text: When a Trainee Is Not Yet Ready
The hardest conversation in training, and the one most often avoided.
Passing someone who is not ready creates a problem on a live project.
It is unfair to the trainees they will go on to teach.
It is unfair to the person, who finds out later and in public.
And it makes every other assessment you give less credible.
What to avoid: softening it until the message disappears, or delivering it as a personal judgement.
A usable form: “You are not yet at the standard for independent work on this task. What I need you to practice is X. We will reassess on Y, and here is what I will be looking for.”
Then record it on the assessment template with the date for reassessment.

Some criteria are passed or they are not. A high overall score does not compensate for failure on a mandatory safety, security or critical annotation requirement — including, on most projects, guessing rather than escalating on an item the guideline does not cover.
Not ready is a statement about this attempt, not about the person. Say what to practice, and when you will look again.
notes:
Rehearse the wording with the room. Most participants have never had to say this and will soften it into meaninglessness the first time.
The critical-criteria definition is worth reading aloud. It is the reason a 9 out of 10 can still be a fail.
Stress the final point: the judgement is about the attempt, with a route back. That is what makes it deliverable without damaging the relationship.

title: Preparation and Peer Coaching
text: Finish the session you built this morning, rehearse it once, and coach a partner through theirs.
notes:
Protected preparation time. Resist filling it with more content — the value is in the rehearsal and the peer coaching.
Confirm the 13:00 running order before this block ends.

title: The Peer Coaching Protocol
text: Fifteen minutes, both partners. Short, structured and specific — this is not a general discussion.
Deliver a two-minute extract.  Not the whole session. Choose the part you are least sure about.
Partner gives three-part feedback.  What was correct, what needs improvement, and how — in that order.
Swap roles and repeat.  Keep to time, or only one of you benefits.
Each person names one change.  One concrete thing you will do differently at 13:00.
Write it on your plan.  A change you did not write down is a change you will not make.
Coach the work, not the person. One specific improvement, not five. Say how, not just what. Keep to time.
Do not rewrite your partner’s session. Do not give only praise. Do not spend the whole slot on one person.
Coaching a peer is itself assessed on Day 3. How you give feedback is as visible as how you deliver.
notes:
Hold the two-minute extract strictly. Partners who deliver the whole session leave no time to swap.
Listen for feedback that is only positive and intervene where you hear it.
The written change in step 5 is what converts coaching into a different delivery at 13:00.

title: Delivering Your Lesson
text: Each participant demonstrates a labelling task and responds to simulated learner questions. This is the assessed delivery.
notes:
Set the tone before the first delivery: a professional rehearsal, not a performance. Observers are an audience of learners and should behave as trainees would.
Confirm the running order and hold the time.

title: What Happens in Your Slot
text: State your objective in one observable sentence.
Demonstrate the labelling task on the platform.
Observers will ask simulated learner questions.
Answer as you would answer a real trainee.
It is correct to say you will check and come back — if you then say how.
It is not correct to invent an answer.
You will also score a peer’s practical work.
Record it on the assessment template.
Keep well inside your slot. A session that overruns loses the check of understanding, which is the criterion most participants already lose marks on.

Technical accuracy is not negotiable. A well-delivered session that teaches an incorrect annotation rule is worse than no session, because the error propagates through every trainee that person goes on to teach.
notes:
Assign the simulated questions to specific observers in advance so they arrive naturally rather than all at once. One or two per delivery is enough.
Score immediately after each delivery while it is fresh. Brief verbal feedback to the room, detail in writing.
Watch specifically for the check of understanding; it is the criterion most often missed.

title: Simulated Learner Questions and Model Answers
text: Simulated Learner Questions and Model Answers
These are the questions real trainees ask. Prepare an answer to each before you deliver.
“What do I do if the guideline does not cover this item?”
Stop, record a clarification request, escalate it to the authorised contact and leave the item until you have a decision.
The single most important behaviour. Guessing creates inconsistency that is expensive to correct later.
“Why is my boundary wrong? It looks fine to me.”
Zoom in to at least 200% and check each edge touches the object. Most boundary errors are made at default zoom.
Gives a practisable technique rather than a judgement.
“Can I just copy the shape from the last image?”
You can copy, but the pasted shape still has to satisfy the specification for this object. Check every edge before you submit.
Copying is legitimate; copying without checking is a common source of boundary errors.
“Who decides whether my work is accepted?”
A QA reviewer inspects a sample against the approved guideline and either accepts it or returns it with the error type recorded.
Makes the quality process visible, which reduces the sense that rejection is arbitrary.
“I am slower than everyone else — is that a problem?”
Accuracy first. Speed comes with practice. Tell me where you are losing time and we will look at it together.
Speed pressure produces rework, which costs more capacity than the slower work would have.
The first question is the one you must get right. A trainer who invents an answer rather than escalating has failed the most important part of the assessment, however well the rest was delivered.
notes:
This page is as useful after the programme as during it. Tell participants to keep it.
Assign specific questions to specific observers before the deliveries begin.
The last question is worth discussing if time allows. New annotators consistently believe speed is what is being measured, and the correction has to come from the trainer.

title: The Teach-Back Rubric
text: How your delivery is scored. Five criteria, each 0 to 2, giving a total out of 10.
What the assessor is looking for
Learning objectives are clear and relevant
One observable objective, stated at the start, that matches what is then taught and assessed.
Every rule, category definition and platform step is correct against the approved guideline.
The task is performed and narrated, at a pace the learner can follow, with examples that include a hard case.
Participants are engaged and given practice
The learner attempts the task, not just watches it. Guided practice precedes independent practice.
Understanding is assessed and feedback is constructive
A specific check of understanding, and feedback in three parts with a practicable instruction.
WHERE MARKS ARE MOST OFTEN LOST
Many participants explain and demonstrate well, then close the session without establishing whether anyone learned anything.
notes:
Give participants this page before the deliveries, not after. They assess each other against it.
Agree the 0/1/2 interpretation out loud as you did for the practical rubric.
Written feedback is required for every participant, naming any area needing further practice before independent delivery.

title: Evaluation and Action Planning
text: Evaluate the programme against capability rather than enjoyment, agree what each trainer practices next, and complete the daily report.
notes: Define the distinction up front: a risk might happen, an issue has happened, and a change alters the agreed basis of the work. Participants mix these constantly, and the response to each is different.

title: Evaluating Against Capability
text: A satisfaction score is not an evaluation. Participants can enjoy a session and leave unable to perform the task.
Whether participants achieved the stated learning outcomes.
Whether they can demonstrate the required annotation tasks.
Whether they can teach and assess those tasks accurately.
Whether materials and examples were clear.
Recommended changes to materials and exercises.
A comparison of starting level against final assessment.
Close the loop. Lessons from this cohort should change the materials for the next one; an evaluation that is filed rather than applied has no value.
COLLECT WRITTEN FEEDBACK BEFORE ANYONE LEAVES
Feedback requested afterwards by email rarely arrives. Complete the evaluation form in the room.
notes:
Say who receives the evaluation and when.
If a diagnostic was run on Day 1, show the comparison against today's results. It is the strongest evidence available that the programme worked.
Hand out the evaluation form at the start of this block so people complete it while you work through the action plans.

title: The Daily Report
text: Completed jointly by the facilitators at the end of each training day.
Expected against actual, with reasons for absence.
What was covered, what was cut and why.
Scores per participant against both rubrics. (where applicable)
Platform, access, timing, materials — and how each was handled.
Anything carried forward, with an owner.
Changes to materials, timings or exercises.
Assessment records, action plans and feedback are personal data about identifiable individuals. Store them in the agreed location, restrict access, and retain them only for the agreed period.
Complete the report before leaving the room. It is far harder to reconstruct the next morning.
notes:
Fill this in jointly rather than delegating it to one facilitator.
The issues row is the one the programme owner reads most closely — it is where the next cohort's improvements come from.
Say the data-protection line out loud. Participants will be handling these records themselves once they start delivering training.

title: Day 3 on One Page
text: You are accountable for what you deliver, whoever drafted it.
The whole day, condensed. If you remember nothing else, remember this.
Five parts: objective, teaching steps, sample tasks, practice, assessment.
Write the objective first, content last.
Two-assessor test: would two people judge it the same way?
State → explain → demonstrate → demonstrate slowly → guided practice → independent practice → check.
Do not prompt during independent practice.
Critical criteria are passed or failed.
“Not yet ready” names what to practise and when you will look again.
When the guideline does not cover an item: stop, record a clarification request, escalate it, and leave the item until there is a decision. Teach it, model it, and assess it.

Good for a first draft, observable objectives, practice variations and plausible learner questions. Always verify technical accuracy against the approved guideline. Never paste client data, real annotation items, trainee names or unpublished guidelines into a public tool.
